Herman Webster Mudgett · 1861–1896

H. H. Holmes The record, the wreckage, and the legend built on top of both

He was a swindler first and a murderer second — and the difference matters. A century of retelling turned a Chicago insurance fraudster who killed at least nine people into a phantom with two hundred victims and a purpose-built slaughterhouse. This archive holds the two apart: what the court records, census returns and detective reports actually support, and what the newspapers invented while the ink was still wet.

Why this archive exists

The most famous facts about H. H. Holmes are the ones that aren't true.

Holmes was real, and what he did was genuinely monstrous. He murdered a business partner and three children, and he almost certainly killed a pregnant woman, her small daughter, and at least one young employee. That alone would secure his place in American criminal history.

But he was tried for exactly one murder, and the vast structure that surrounds him in popular memory — the purpose-built killing hotel, the hundreds of vanished fairgoers, the gas lines and dissecting table — was assembled in the late summer of 1895 by Chicago newspapers competing for circulation, then hardened into fact by pulp magazines, mid-century true-crime paperbacks, and finally by a bestselling 2003 narrative history that put him in the same book as the World's Columbian Exposition.6

How this site marks its claims

Every substantive assertion carries a status. Documented means court records, contemporaneous official documents, or physical evidence. Probable means strong circumstantial or multi-source support without a conviction. Disputed means credible historians actively disagree. Invention means it can be traced to a specific piece of fiction or sensational reporting.

Thirty-five years

Open the timeline
I was born with the devil in me. I could not help the fact that I was a murderer, no more than the poet can help the inspiration to sing. H. H. Holmes, confession sold to the Philadelphia Inquirer, April 1896 — a document in which he also claimed to be physically changing shape, and named victims who were subsequently found alive4

The shape of the case

Five moves, and a detective who wouldn't let go

If you read nothing else, read this. It is the entire documented arc.

01 / The pattern

Fraud, not slaughter, was the business

From medical school onward, Holmes ran insurance and credit swindles: buying goods on credit and selling them off, mortgaging the same fixtures repeatedly, and taking out life policies on people who could be made to disappear. Killing was, in his own operating logic, a cost of the scheme — which is exactly why the victim count is smaller and the crimes more calculated than the legend suggests.

02 / The building

He built a block he could not pay for

The three-storey building at 601–603 West 63rd Street went up between 1887 and 1892, financed by unpaid suppliers and rotating contractors. Its oddities — blind corners, a stairway to nowhere, doors that opened onto brick — are as easily explained by a serial debtor endlessly re-partitioning a building to dodge creditors as by a murder architecture. 1

03 / The killings

The Chicago deaths

Julia Smythe Conner and her daughter Pearl vanished around Christmas 1891. Emeline Cigrand, a young stenographer, vanished in December 1892. Both had been close to Holmes; neither was ever traced alive again. These are the deaths the legend expands into hundreds — and the ones for which he was never charged.

04 / The unravelling

A $10,000 policy and a body in Philadelphia

In September 1894 Benjamin Pitezel, Holmes's long-time accomplice, was found dead in a Callowhill Street house, staged as a laboratory accident. The insurance payout was collected. When the fraud was detected, Holmes took three of Pitezel's children on a months-long circuit of American and Canadian cities — and arrived without them.

05 / The reckoning

Detective Frank Geyer, and 900 boarding houses

Philadelphia detective Frank P. Geyer spent the summer of 1895 retracing Holmes's route through Cincinnati, Indianapolis, Detroit and Toronto with photographs of the children, knocking on doors until the trail closed. He found Alice and Nellie Pitezel buried in a cellar on St. Vincent Street in Toronto that July, and Howard's remains in a rented cottage in Irvington, Indiana, in August. Geyer's methodical account is the single most reliable document in the entire case.2

Context

The White City, and why the fair keeps getting blamed

Between May and October 1893, some twenty-seven million admissions were recorded at the World's Columbian Exposition in Jackson Park — a temporary city of white stucco palaces six miles from Holmes's building. Chicago swelled with strangers who had no local relatives to report them missing. It is an irresistible setting, and the pairing of the fair with the killer is now so fixed that most people assume it is the core of the case.

It is not. The best modern documentary work — including a systematic review of building permits, city directories, licences and newspaper advertising — indicates that the upper floors were never running as a functioning hotel during the exposition, and that no contemporaneous record connects a single fair visitor to the building.1 The fair is context. It is not evidence.

Where the pairing comes from

The fair-and-the-killer structure is a narrative device, popularised by Erik Larson's The Devil in the White City (2003), which interleaves Holmes's story with that of the exposition's architect Daniel Burnham. Larson's book is carefully sourced but built on the surviving 1890s press record, and it is a work of narrative history, not a forensic audit. Its structure — not its claims — is what most people now remember as fact.

A note on reading this

The real man is more interesting than the monster

Strip away the trapdoors and the crematorium and you are left with something harder to look at: an ordinary-seeming, sociable, well-spoken pharmacist who killed people because it was administratively convenient, and who was caught not by genius but by a stubborn detective with a stack of photographs and a railway timetable.

Nine people are named in this archive. Where the record allows it, they are described as they lived rather than as they were found.

I

Chapter one

A life in fragments

Almost everything Holmes said about himself was a lie, including the autobiography he sold for money while awaiting execution. What follows is built from the parts that can be checked: registers, deeds, licences, marriage records, and the testimony of people who had no reason to invent.

Gilmanton, New Hampshire

Herman Webster Mudgett was born on 16 May 1861 in Gilmanton, a farming town in the Belknap County hills, to Levi Horton Mudgett and Theodate Page Price. The family was old New England stock and rigidly Methodist. He was the third of four children, bright, physically slight, and — by every account including his own — set apart from other boys in the village.

The most famous story of his childhood comes from his own 1895 memoir: that schoolmates, knowing he was frightened of the village doctor's office, dragged him inside and forced him face to face with a skeleton, and that the terror turned instantly into fascination. It is a perfect origin story, which is precisely the problem — it appears nowhere but in a document he wrote to be sold, and it does the convenient work of explaining him without implicating him.4

Treat the memoir as evidence of Holmes, not of events

Holmes' Own Story (1895) and the confession he sold to Hearst's papers in 1896 are the two richest-sounding sources on his early life and the two least reliable. He contradicts himself between them, invents victims, and in the confession claims his own face was physically elongating into a devil's. They are useful for understanding how he wanted to be seen. They are worthless as chronology.

On 4 July 1878, aged seventeen, he married Clara A. Lovering in Alton, New Hampshire. They had a son, Robert. Holmes never divorced her. She would learn what he had become from newspapers, seventeen years later.

Ann Arbor and the corpse trade

After teaching school in Gilmanton and later in Vermont, Mudgett enrolled at the University of Michigan's Department of Medicine and Surgery in Ann Arbor, graduating in June 1884. The medical training is genuine and documented, and it matters: it gave him anatomical knowledge, access to chemicals, the vocabulary of a professional man, and — critically — a working familiarity with how bodies were procured, handled and disposed of by institutions.

Michigan in the 1880s ran a large dissection programme, and cadavers moved through a grey market. The persistent story is that Mudgett stole bodies from the medical school, disfigured them, and used them to claim on life insurance policies taken out on invented people. No prosecution followed and no contemporaneous record confirms it; the account traces largely to his own later boasting and to press reconstruction after his arrest. What is firmly established is that the identical scheme — a fraudulent death claim supported by a substitute corpse — was the one he tried to run in Philadelphia ten years later, and that this time it was documented in exhaustive detail by prosecutors.

The insurance fraud was not a phase he passed through on the way to murder. It was the whole architecture. Murder was what happened when a body was required and no substitute was available.

Chicago, and the name

Mudgett surfaced in Chicago in 1886 under a new name: Henry Howard Holmes. The choice was not accidental — Conan Doyle's detective had appeared in print the following year and the surname carried a whiff of respectable professionalism. He took work at a drugstore on the corner of South Wallace Avenue and West 63rd Street in Englewood, then an independent township recently annexed to the city, run by Elizabeth S. Holton, whose husband was seriously ill.

The legend says he murdered the Holtons and seized the store. He did not. Mrs. Holton outlived him by decades; the property transfer was a purchase, and the dispute that followed was a mundane commercial one about unpaid notes. The correction matters because it is the first place the legend departs from the record, and because it establishes the actual pattern: Holmes acquired things by paperwork and nerve, not violence, until paperwork stopped working.

Status: documented

Elizabeth Holton's survival is confirmed by census returns and by her own later statements to the press. The "he killed the pharmacist's widow" version appears in 1895 newspaper coverage and has been repeated continuously since.1

Three wives, none of them ended

Holmes married three times and divorced no one. The bigamy is not incidental colour; it is the clearest available window into how he operated — parallel lives, each maintained with total conviction, each with its own address, finances and future plans.

The three marriages of H. H. Holmes
WifeMarriedWhereOutcome
Clara A. Lovering 4 July 1878 Alton, New Hampshire Never divorced. One son, Robert. Effectively abandoned by 1885.
Myrta Z. Belknap 28 January 1887 Minneapolis, Minnesota Bigamous. One daughter, Lucy. Settled in Wilmette; Holmes visited intermittently and she appears to have believed in his respectability to the end.
Georgiana Yoke 17 January 1894 Denver, Colorado Bigamous. Married under the alias Henry Mansfield Howard. Travelled with him during the Pitezel period and testified at his trial.

There was a fourth relationship of the same kind, unmarried but presented as marriage: Julia Smythe Conner, whose husband Ned worked in the jewellery counter of Holmes's store. Ned left. Julia and her daughter Pearl stayed. Neither was seen after Christmas 1891.

The manner

Almost everyone who met Holmes and lived described the same man: courteous, softly spoken, unusually attentive, physically unremarkable at about five feet eight, with a heavy moustache and eyes that people kept describing as startlingly pale and steady. He paid compliments. He remembered details. He was extraordinarily good at getting credit extended.

Creditors' letters, supplier lawsuits and the reminiscences of former employees sketch a man perpetually one week ahead of collapse: furniture bought on credit and immediately resold; the same fixtures mortgaged to three different lenders; a glass-bending machine and a "copier" company and a mail- order cure for alcoholism, all of them vehicles for taking money in advance. By 1893 he was being sued from several directions at once, and a creditor's agent named he could not shake had begun assembling a case against him.

Flight

In the summer of 1894 Holmes left Chicago for good. The building on 63rd Street was mortgaged past its value and under investigation; a fire in August 1895 — after his arrest — damaged the upper floors and was itself widely suspected to be one of his insurance plays, arranged in advance.

He surfaced in Fort Worth, Texas, working a land scheme with Benjamin Pitezel, then in St. Louis, where he was briefly jailed for a drugstore swindle. It was in that St. Louis cell, awaiting bail, that he shared a wing with the train robber Marion Hedgepeth and described a plan: fake a death, collect ten thousand dollars in life insurance, split the proceeds. Hedgepeth would supply a crooked lawyer for a five-hundred-dollar cut.

Holmes never paid him. Hedgepeth wrote to the authorities. Every subsequent thing that happened to Holmes proceeded from that unpaid five hundred dollars.

Continue

The Pitezel scheme, the disappearance of three children, and the transcontinental pursuit that followed are covered in Manhunt & Trial. The building he left behind is mapped in The Castle.

What he probably was

Retrospective diagnosis across 130 years is unreliable and this archive will not pretend otherwise. What can be said descriptively is that the record shows a consistent, lifelong pattern: instrumental deceit sustained over years, absence of durable attachment, parallel identities maintained without apparent strain, and violence deployed without evident emotion when a person became an obstacle or an asset. He killed children in his care and then wrote a memoir complaining about his treatment in prison.

The confessions are worth one last note. Holmes confessed repeatedly, in mutually contradictory versions, escalating the count each time and always for payment. At least two people he "confessed" to murdering read about their own deaths in the newspaper and came forward alive. He was, to the end, doing the only thing he had ever reliably done well: selling a story to a buyer who wanted it.

II

Chapter two

The building on 63rd Street

Nobody called it the Murder Castle until the newspapers did, in August 1895, three years after it was finished and a year after Holmes had abandoned it. This is what stood there, floor by floor — and where the record stops and the invention starts.

1887–92 Built In stages, as money and credit allowed.

What the searchers actually found

When Chicago police finally searched the building in July and August 1895 — prompted not by any Chicago investigation but by the Philadelphia case against Holmes — they were working inside a partially unfinished, heavily re-partitioned commercial block that had stood empty and mortgaged for a year.

What they recorded was strange. What the newspapers printed was stranger, and arrived faster. Pick a room to see which is which.

How a mortgaged building became a machine

On 20 July 1895 the Chicago police, acting on information from Philadelphia, entered the building. Within days the story had escaped entirely. The Chicago Tribune, the Times-Herald, the Inter Ocean and the New York papers were competing daily, and each new edition needed a new horror. Reporters were given the run of the place. Diagrams were drawn from memory and imagination. Features appeared in print that had not been in the previous day's account of the same room.

By the time the excavation ended, the building had acquired a gas chamber, a crematorium, a soundproof vault, an elevator for bodies, and a hundred-odd victims. None of it was evidence. All of it was printed as fact, and it is the version that survived, because it was the version that was fun to read.

It is worth being precise about what this correction does and does not do. It does not exonerate Holmes: he murdered people, including children, and the vault on the second floor is a genuinely sinister object. It corrects the scale and the mechanism — from an industrial killing plant to a fraudster's decaying building where several people died and were concealed.

Summary

The building, feature by feature

Every element of the Castle legend, graded against the surviving record.

Assessment of features attributed to the Holmes building
Feature Status Assessment
Three-storey mixed-use block Documented Built 1887–92, shops below, rooms above. Real, and unremarkable for Englewood.
Constant re-partitioning; unpaid contractors Documented Multiple builders, none paid in full, none with sight of the whole job. Attested by suppliers and lawsuits.
Windowless rooms, blind doors, stair to nowhere Real; purpose disputed The oddities existed. Whether they were designed as traps or left by chaotic renovation is the live question.
Airtight vault beside the office Probable Reported with a gas fitting and a footprint on the inside of the door. The most credible sinister feature.
Basement remains Partly documented Bone fragments and clothing recovered. No identification, no cause of death, no charge.
Goods shaft / "body chute" Disputed A shaft existed. Every commercial block had one. Its use is unrecorded.
Crematory furnace Largely invention A domestic stove cannot cremate a body. Probably the glass-bending kiln he had sold to investors.
Central gas-control panel Invention Never produced, never photographed, never entered in evidence, never testified to by any fitter.
Soundproof asbestos chamber Invention Asbestos was standard fireproofing. The interpretation was the reporter's contribution.
Operating hotel full of fairgoers Not supported Advertised, licence sought; no evidence of operation, no documented guest, no traced victim.

III

Chapter three

The register of the dead

Nine people. Not a number — nine people, most of whom knew him well and trusted him, four of them children. Where the record permits, they are described here as they lived.

On counting

Holmes confessed to twenty-seven murders and the legend claims two hundred. The confession was written for payment, lists people who were later found alive, and contradicts his own earlier statements. The two-hundred figure has never been traced to any source at all. This register lists only people whose existence and disappearance are independently documented and whose deaths are attributable to Holmes on evidence — a standard that yields nine names, and that will grow if better evidence ever emerges.

SHOWING 9 OF 9 RECORDS

Julia Smythe Conner c. 1860 – December 1891 · aged c. 31
Probable

A tall, striking woman from Davenport, Iowa, who came to Chicago when her husband Ned took a job at the jewellery counter in Holmes's building. She worked in the store, kept its books, and was capable enough that Holmes made her a manager. He also began an affair with her, in full view; Ned left in 1891. Julia stayed on with her daughter.

She was reportedly pregnant when she disappeared around Christmas 1891. Holmes later gave several accounts, including that she died during an abortion he performed. Neither she nor Pearl was ever seen again, and no death record exists for either.

ChicagoNo body identifiedNever charged
Pearl Conner c. 1883 – December 1891 · aged c. 8
Probable

Julia's daughter, and the first child. She lived in the building with her mother and was, by the accounts of tenants, a familiar presence around the shops. She vanished at the same time as Julia and for the same reason: she was a witness.

In one version of his confession Holmes admitted killing them both. In another he denied it entirely. Pearl has no grave, no death certificate, and for most of the last century no place in the story except as a subordinate clause.

ChicagoChildNo body identified
Emeline Cigrand c. 1868 – December 1892 · aged c. 24
Probable

A stenographer from Lafayette, Indiana, described by everyone who knew her as exceptionally attractive and exceptionally competent. She had been working at the Keeley Institute in Dwight, Illinois — the famous alcoholism-cure sanatorium — when Holmes recruited her to his office in the spring of 1892 at a conspicuously good salary.

She wrote to her family about an engagement to a wealthy man named Robert Phelps. In December 1892 the letters stopped. Her family's enquiries went nowhere, and it was only after 1895 that they learned who her employer had been.

ChicagoNo body identifiedNever charged
Benjamin F. Pitezel 1857 – 2 September 1894 · aged 37
Convicted

A carpenter from Illinois and Holmes's accomplice for years — the man who fronted schemes, signed papers, and did the work. He drank heavily, had a wife, Carrie, and five children, and appears to have believed to the very last that he was a partner rather than a commodity.

The plan was that Pitezel would fake his own death and the family would collect $10,000. Instead Holmes killed him — chloroform, the post-mortem found, administered while he was insensible with drink — and staged the body in the back room of 1316 Callowhill Street, Philadelphia, as the victim of an exploded laboratory lamp. The insurance was paid out. This is the one murder for which Holmes stood trial, was convicted, and was hanged.

PhiladelphiaBody identifiedConvicted 2 Nov 1895
Alice Pitezel 1879 – c. 25 October 1894 · aged 15
Documented

The eldest Pitezel daughter, and the reason so much of this story can be reconstructed at all: Alice wrote letters. She wrote to her mother from Indianapolis, from Detroit, from Toronto — careful, homesick, dutiful letters describing the hotels and the weather and asking when they would all be together again.

Holmes collected the letters and never posted them. They were found among his effects and read aloud in court, and they remain the most devastating documents in the case. She and her sister were suffocated in the cellar of a rented house at 16 St. Vincent Street, Toronto, where Detective Geyer found them on 15 July 1895.

TorontoChildBody recovered 15 Jul 1895
Nellie Pitezel 1883 – c. 25 October 1894 · aged 11
Documented

The middle child of the three taken. She had long braids, which Holmes cut off before the burial in an attempt to hinder identification — a detail Geyer recorded flatly and which did more than any rhetoric to fix the case in the public mind.

The two sisters were buried together in a shallow hole in the cellar of the Toronto house. Holmes had rented the house, borrowed a spade from the neighbour next door, and returned it.

TorontoChildBody recovered 15 Jul 1895
Howard Pitezel 1886 – c. October 1894 · aged 8
Documented

The only boy, and the first of the three to be killed — separated from his sisters at Indianapolis, which is why Alice's later letters keep asking after him. Holmes found him difficult to manage and said so.

Geyer traced a cottage Holmes had rented in Irvington, on the eastern edge of Indianapolis, and on 27 August 1895 found charred remains, teeth and a piece of a toy in the chimney and stove. The boy's identity was confirmed in part by the toy, which his mother recognised.

Irvington, Ind.ChildRemains recovered 27 Aug 1895
Minnie R. Williams c. 1869 – c. 1893 · aged c. 24
Probable

A Texas heiress who came into a Fort Worth property inheritance and into Holmes's orbit around 1893. She worked in the building, was introduced as his wife, and signed the Texas property over to a Holmes alias — after which the Fort Worth land scheme with Pitezel became possible.

She disappeared in 1893. Holmes's story was that she had gone to Europe; later he claimed she had killed her own sister and fled, a version no one has ever corroborated. The property transfer supplies both the motive and the paper trail.

Chicago / Fort WorthNo body identifiedNever charged
Anna "Nannie" Williams c. 1871 – c. July 1893 · aged c. 22
Probable

Minnie's younger sister, a schoolteacher from Midlothian, Texas, who came north to visit and to see the World's Columbian Exposition. She wrote home about the fair and about her sister's impressive fiancé.

Her letters stop in the summer of 1893. Both sisters vanish from the record at effectively the same moment, in the same city, in the same building, with the same man in possession of their property afterwards. She is the closest thing the case has to a genuine World's Fair victim — and even she was not a stranger passing through, but a guest who knew her host.

ChicagoNo body identifiedNever charged

The ones who weren't

A register of victims is only honest if it also records who has been wrongly added to it. Several names carried for a century in books and documentaries do not survive checking.

Elizabeth S. Holton, the pharmacist's wife from whom Holmes took over the drugstore, is routinely listed as his first murder. She outlived him. Robert Phelps, the wealthy fiancé Emeline Cigrand wrote home about, appears never to have existed at all — the name was almost certainly one of Holmes's own inventions. Several of the twenty-seven people named in the 1896 confession read about their own deaths in the papers and wrote in to say they were fine.

And there is the darkest possibility in the other direction: Carrie Pitezel, Benjamin's widow, survived — but she spent months travelling the same circuit as Holmes, one or two cities behind her own children, believing she was being taken to meet them. She was in Detroit at the same time as her daughters, a few streets away, while Holmes moved between the two parties. Geyer's account of telling her what he had found in Toronto is the hardest passage in the literature.

IV

Chapter four

Geyer's manhunt

Holmes was not caught by brilliant detection of his murders. He was caught because he cheated a train robber out of five hundred dollars, and then because one Philadelphia detective refused to accept that three children could simply stop existing.

The $10,000 policy

The plan Holmes described in a St. Louis jail cell in 1894 was simple and not original. Benjamin Pitezel would take out a life insurance policy for $10,000 with the Fidelity Mutual Life Association, set himself up in Philadelphia as a patent promoter under the name B. F. Perry, and then "die" in a laboratory accident. A substitute corpse would be produced. Pitezel's wife Carrie would identify it and collect. Holmes would take his share.

Marion Hedgepeth, the train robber sharing the wing, agreed to supply a crooked lawyer in exchange for $500. Holmes took the introduction and never paid.

On 4 September 1894 a body was found in the back room of 1316 Callowhill Street, burned about the face and chest, beside a broken bottle and a pipe. It was ruled accidental. The claim was filed. And no substitute corpse was ever involved: the body was Pitezel himself, chloroformed while insensibly drunk and then arranged.

The letter

From prison, Hedgepeth wrote to the authorities describing the scheme and naming Holmes. That letter reached the insurance company, which had already begun to have doubts, and the company put a detective on it. Holmes was arrested in Boston on 17 November 1894 — not for murder, but on an outstanding warrant for horse theft out of Fort Worth, Texas.

At that point everyone believed the case was an insurance fraud with one suspicious death. Nobody was looking for children.

The people who ended it

Marion Hedgepeth

Train robber. Wrote the letter that started everything, over an unpaid $500. Received a commutation for it, and was shot dead by a policeman in a Chicago saloon robbery in 1910.

W. E. Gary & Fidelity Mutual

The insurer that declined to quietly absorb a suspicious claim and instead paid for the investigation that exposed it.

Frank P. Geyer

Philadelphia detective, twenty years' service, recently bereaved of his own wife and daughter in a house fire. Given the file nobody expected to close.

Carrie Pitezel

Benjamin's widow. Handed three of her five children to Holmes and was moved around the country for months believing she was about to be reunited with them.

Summer 1895

Nine hundred boarding houses

Geyer left Philadelphia on 26 June 1895 with photographs of Alice, Nellie and Howard Pitezel and a bundle of Holmes's aliases. He had no forensic science, no national database and no jurisdiction outside Pennsylvania. He had train timetables, hotel registers, and the willingness to knock on every door in a city.

26 June 1895Cincinnati

The first trace

Working from hotel registers, Geyer establishes that Holmes and three children stayed in Cincinnati in late September 1894 under assorted names, and that Holmes rented a house on Poplar Street — into which he had a stove delivered, and then abruptly gave the house up. A neighbour had thought the delivery of a large stove for a man with no furniture peculiar enough to remember it.

Early July 1895Indianapolis

Howard separates from his sisters

Geyer traces the party to Indianapolis hotels, and finds that from a certain date onward only two children are recorded. Alice's undelivered letters, read alongside the registers, show her asking repeatedly after her brother. Geyer searches Indianapolis exhaustively and finds nothing. He moves on.

Mid July 1895Detroit

Three parties, one man

In Detroit, Geyer establishes the fact that defines the whole pursuit: Holmes had the two girls at one address, Carrie Pitezel and her remaining children at a second, and his wife Georgiana Yoke at a third — simultaneously, moving between them, keeping a mother within walking distance of daughters she was told she would see tomorrow.

15 July 1895Toronto

16 St. Vincent Street

Geyer and Toronto detective Alfred Cuddy work through the city's rental agents. They find a house Holmes rented in October 1894 for a fortnight. The neighbour recalls lending him a spade. In the cellar, under three feet of earth, Geyer finds Alice and Nellie Pitezel. Nellie's braids had been cut off and buried with them.

27 August 1895Irvington, Indiana

The cottage and the stove

Geyer returns to Indiana and starts again, this time on the outlying villages. In Irvington, a resident remembers a man who rented a cottage and asked repeatedly about the chimney. In the chimney and the stove Geyer finds charred bone, teeth, and a scorched tin toy that Carrie Pitezel identifies as Howard's.

July–August 1895Chicago

Meanwhile, the building

As Geyer's findings reach the papers, Chicago police open the 63rd Street building. Within a fortnight the excavation has become a national spectacle and the "Murder Castle" has been invented in print. No Chicago prosecution ever results — but this is the moment the legend outgrows the case, and it has never stopped growing since.

The trial

Commonwealth of Pennsylvania v. Herman W. Mudgett, alias H. H. Holmes opened in Philadelphia on 28 October 1895 before Judge Michael Arnold. The charge was the murder of Benjamin F. Pitezel — one count, one victim, no mention of Chicago.

The prosecution's case was medical and documentary: the post-mortem finding of chloroform in quantities inconsistent with an accident and with the position of the body; the staged scene; the insurance paperwork; and above all the identification evidence tying Holmes to every stage of the fraud.

Holmes dismissed his counsel on the second day and conducted his own defence for a period — cross-examining witnesses competently, by most accounts, and then allowing his lawyers to return. Georgiana Yoke, his third wife, testified. Carrie Pitezel testified. The verdict came on 2 November 1895 after deliberation reported at under three hours: guilty of murder in the first degree.

Appeals to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court and a clemency petition to the governor both failed.

The confessions

In April 1896, from his cell, Holmes sold a confession to the Hearst press — reportedly for around $7,500, a fortune at the time. In it he admitted twenty-seven murders and described his own body physically deforming into something devilish.

The document collapsed almost immediately. Named victims turned up alive. Dates contradicted verifiable records. He had already given at least two other, incompatible accounts. It remains the single most quoted source about him and the single least reliable, and virtually every inflated victim count in circulation descends from it.

What the conviction rests on

Chloroform found in the stomach in a quantity and distribution inconsistent with the staged accident; a body position inconsistent with the scene; the insurance application, correspondence and payout in Holmes's hand or under his direction; and the subsequent conduct — the removal of the children — as evidence of consciousness of guilt.

7 May 1896

Holmes was hanged in the yard of Moyamensing Prison, Philadelphia, on the morning of 7 May 1896, nine days before his thirty-fifth birthday. He was calm, spoke briefly, and used his last statement to retract the confession — saying he had killed only two women, by botched abortions, and no one else. It was the final version, and no more reliable than the others.

The drop was short and the fall did not break his neck cleanly. He was reported to have taken something over fifteen minutes to die, and was pronounced dead about twenty minutes after the trap opened.

He had left precise instructions for his burial, and they were followed: no embalming, a coffin filled with cement, the grave dug to twice the usual depth and topped with a further layer of concrete, in an unmarked plot at Holy Cross Cemetery in Yeadon, Delaware County. The usual explanation is that he feared grave-robbing by medical schools — the trade he had himself worked in.

The 2017 exhumation

The concrete grave fed a durable rumour that Holmes bribed his way out and sent another man to the gallows. In 2017, at the request of his descendants and with court authorisation, the grave was opened. The coffin had to be cut out of solid cement. The remains inside were badly decomposed but the teeth and the moustache were intact, and dental comparison identified them as Holmes.

He was hanged, he stayed buried, and he is still there.

Afterwards

A superstition grew that everyone connected with the case met a bad end — the warden, the priest, the jury foreman, the coroner, the arresting officer. The list circulates constantly and does not survive checking: several of the named men lived long, unremarkable lives, and Frank Geyer, the most exposed of them all, went on to a comfortable career in insurance investigation and died of natural causes in 1918.

The building burned, was patched, stood for forty more years, and came down in 1938. The legend, which needed no building, has done considerably better.

Open the myth check
V

Chapter five

Myth check

Twelve claims you have almost certainly heard, each traced back to where it actually came from. Two of them turn out to be true. One is true but for the wrong reasons. The rest are newspaper copy that outlived its newspapers.

0 Hold up
0 Partly true
0 Do not survive checking

✕  No documentary basis whatsoever

This is the number that appears on documentary posters and in encyclopaedia entries, and it has no source. It cannot be traced to any statement by Holmes, any police estimate, any coroner, or any court. It appears to have emerged from pulp true-crime writing in the twentieth century, where each retelling rounded the previous one upward.

The highest figure Holmes himself ever gave was twenty-seven, in a confession he was paid for, and several of those twenty-seven were subsequently found alive. The number this archive can defend is nine.

✕  Not supported by the records

He did advertise lodging and did pursue a hotel licence. But research through city licensing files, directories, insurance maps and newspaper advertising has failed to establish that the upper floors ever operated as a working hotel during the exposition, and not one missing fair visitor has ever been documented as having stayed there.1

The building was six miles from Jackson Park, in a residential district, and was still partly unfinished. The fair-hotel image is the load-bearing wall of the entire legend, and it is the part with the least underneath it.

◐  A real vault; an invented apparatus

The centralised control panel — a board of valves letting Holmes gas any room at will — was never produced in evidence, never photographed, and never testified to by any gasfitter or plumber who had worked on the building. It is a newspaper construction of August 1895.

What does appear to have existed is a single large airtight closet or vault adjoining his office, with a gas fitting serving it, and a bare footprint reported on the inside of the door. That is a far smaller claim than the legend, and considerably more disturbing.

✕  Misread objects

Cremation requires sustained temperatures around 800–1,000°C for hours. A domestic coal stove of the 1890s does not come close, and the object found in the basement is at least as consistent with the glass-bending kiln Holmes had been promoting to investors as with anything else.

The "acid vat" was reported as quicklime, which is not a body-disposal agent at all: it slows decomposition, which is exactly why it was used in mass graves to suppress odour. A lime pit in a building under five years of continuous plastering is unremarkable.

◐  The oddities were real; the purpose is contested

Windowless rooms, doors opening onto brick and a stair rising into a sealed ceiling are all attested by people who worked in and searched the building. Holmes really did hire and fire contractors constantly so that no single builder saw the whole job.

But there is a second, duller explanation that fits every fact: a man five years deep in debt, endlessly re-partitioning his own building to create new lettable rooms, dodging suppliers, and abandoning half-finished plans when the money ran out. The contractor churn is at least as well explained by not paying them as by concealment. Both readings remain live.

✕  She outlived him

Elizabeth S. Holton appears in later census returns and gave statements to the press after Holmes's arrest. The store changed hands by purchase, and the subsequent dispute was a commercial one over unpaid notes.

This is a useful test case: it is one of the very first things most accounts say about him, it has been repeated for over a century, and it is flatly false.

✕  No

Promoted in a 2017 television series and a book by a descendant, the theory requires Holmes to have been in Whitechapel during the autumn of 1888. The documentary record places him in the United States across that period — trading, marrying, appearing in city directories and pursuing business in Chicago.

The claimed handwriting match has not been accepted by document examiners, and the crimes have nothing in common in method, victim profile or motive: the Ripper killings were frenzied street attacks on strangers; Holmes killed people he knew, for money, indoors, and hid the bodies.

✕  Settled in 2017

The rumour was fed by the concrete-filled grave he requested. In 2017 the grave at Holy Cross Cemetery was opened under court authorisation at the request of his descendants. The coffin had to be cut free of solid cement.

The remains were decomposed, but the teeth and moustache survived, and dental comparison identified them as Holmes. He was hanged on 7 May 1896 and he is still in the ground in Delaware County.

✓  True — and worthless as evidence

He did write and sell that confession, in April 1896, reportedly for around $7,500. So the claim is literally accurate.

It is also the most misleading true statement in the case. He confessed multiple times in mutually contradictory versions; at least two named "victims" turned up alive; the dates conflict with verifiable records; and he withdrew the whole thing on the scaffold. Every subsequent inflated count in popular culture traces back to a document its own author repudiated.

✓  Documented in full

This is the part of the story people find hardest to believe and it is the best-evidenced thing he ever did. Alice and Nellie Pitezel were recovered from the cellar of 16 St. Vincent Street, Toronto, on 15 July 1895 by Detective Frank Geyer. Howard's remains were recovered from a chimney and stove in Irvington, Indiana, on 27 August 1895.

Geyer's book documents the search step by step, city by city, and remains the single most reliable source in the entire literature.2

✕  Survivorship bias with a list attached

The "Holmes curse" list circulates in a fairly fixed form: the trial judge, the jury foreman, the coroner, the priest, the arresting officer, all dead in strange circumstances. Checked individually, several of them lived long and entirely ordinary lives, and the deaths that did occur were unremarkable for men of that age in that era.

Frank Geyer — the person most deeply immersed in the case — retired comfortably into insurance investigation and died of natural causes in 1918.

◐  A marketing phrase, not a fact

The Bloody Benders of Kansas were killing travellers in the early 1870s. The Harpe brothers were killing along the frontier in the 1790s. Serial murder was not invented in Englewood in 1891, and the term "serial killer" itself did not enter common use until the 1970s.

What is defensible is narrower and more interesting: Holmes was arguably America's first mass-media serial killer — the first whose case was covered nationally, daily, by competing wire-served newspapers, and therefore the first to be turned into a product while the trial was still running. The distortion is not a later corruption of his story. It is his story.

✦

A caution about this page

Debunking has its own momentum, and it is possible to over-correct into implying that Holmes was merely a swindler who got a bad press. He was not. He chloroformed his own accomplice, then took that man's three children across two countries and killed all of them, and buried two girls under a rented cellar floor with a borrowed spade. The corrections on this page reduce the scale of his crimes. They do not soften them.

Open the timeline
VI

Chapter six

Thirty-five years

From a farmhouse in Belknap County to a concrete grave outside Philadelphia — and then a hundred and thirty years in which the story kept growing without him.

SHOWING 32 ENTRIES

Origins

1861 – 1886
16 May 1861Gilmanton, N.H.

Herman Webster Mudgett is born

Third child of Levi Horton Mudgett and Theodate Page Price, in a strict Methodist farming household. The American Civil War is five weeks old.

4 July 1878Alton, N.H.

Marries Clara A. Lovering

He is seventeen. One son, Robert, follows. He never divorces her, and she learns what he became from newspapers in 1895.

1882 – June 1884Ann Arbor, Mich.

University of Michigan medical school

Graduates in medicine and surgery. Gains anatomical training, pharmaceutical knowledge, and a professional bearing he uses for the rest of his life. Later boasts — uncorroborated — of running cadaver insurance frauds while enrolled.

1885 – 1886New York / Philadelphia / Chicago

Becomes H. H. Holmes

Abandons Clara, drifts through a series of towns and short-lived jobs, and adopts the name Henry Howard Holmes. Arrives in Chicago.

Englewood

1886 – 1893
188663rd & Wallace, Chicago

Takes over the Holton drugstore

Employed by, then buying out, Elizabeth S. Holton. Contrary to the legend, she outlives him by decades; the ensuing dispute is about unpaid notes, not murder.

28 January 1887Minneapolis, Minn.

Marries Myrta Belknap — bigamously

Still married to Clara. A daughter, Lucy, is born; Myrta is installed in Wilmette and largely kept apart from the Englewood business.

1887 – 1892601–603 W. 63rd St.

The building goes up

Three storeys and a basement, built in stages on credit, with contractors hired and dismissed continuously and few of them ever paid in full. This is the structure the press will christen the Murder Castle eight years later.

December 1891Chicago

Julia and Pearl Conner disappear

Julia — his bookkeeper, his mistress, and reportedly pregnant — and her eight-year-old daughter are never seen again. No death records exist for either. No charge is ever brought.

Spring 1892Dwight → Chicago, Ill.

Emeline Cigrand is hired

Recruited from the Keeley Institute as a stenographer at a conspicuously generous salary. She writes home about an engagement to a wealthy Robert Phelps — a man who appears never to have existed.

December 1892Chicago

Emeline Cigrand disappears

The letters to Lafayette, Indiana, stop. Her family's enquiries lead nowhere for three years.

1 May – 30 Oct 1893Jackson Park, Chicago

The World's Columbian Exposition

Twenty-seven million admissions to a temporary white city six miles east of the building. Holmes advertises lodging; no record establishes that his upper floors ever operated as a hotel, and no fair visitor has ever been documented as a victim.

1893Chicago / Fort Worth, Tex.

Minnie and Anna Williams vanish

Minnie signs her Texas inheritance over to a Holmes alias, then disappears with her visiting sister. The Fort Worth property becomes the basis of the next scheme.

The Pitezel scheme

1894
17 January 1894Denver, Colo.

Marries Georgiana Yoke — bigamously, again

Under the alias Henry Mansfield Howard, while both earlier wives are living. She will travel with him through the Pitezel period and testify at his trial.

July 1894St. Louis, Mo.

Jailed for a drugstore swindle — and meets Hedgepeth

In the cell he describes the insurance plan to train robber Marion Hedgepeth and promises $500 for the introduction to a crooked lawyer. He never pays it. That unpaid debt destroys him.

2–4 September 18941316 Callowhill St., Philadelphia

Benjamin Pitezel is murdered

Chloroformed while insensible with drink, then staged as the victim of an exploded laboratory lamp. Ruled accidental. The $10,000 policy is claimed and paid.

October 1894Indianapolis → Toronto

The three children

Holmes takes Alice, Nellie and Howard Pitezel on a circuit of cities, moving them separately from their mother. Howard is killed near Indianapolis; Alice and Nellie in a rented Toronto cellar. Alice's letters home are collected by Holmes and never posted.

17 November 1894Boston, Mass.

Arrested

Taken on an outstanding Fort Worth horse-theft warrant after Hedgepeth's letter reaches the authorities and Fidelity Mutual's own investigators close in. Nobody is yet looking for the children.

The pursuit and the trial

1895
26 June 1895Philadelphia

Detective Frank Geyer sets out

With photographs of three children and a list of aliases, no jurisdiction outside Pennsylvania, and no expectation of success.

Late June – July 1895Cincinnati · Indianapolis · Detroit

The trail through the hotel registers

Geyer reconstructs the route from lodging books and rental agents, and establishes that in Detroit Holmes kept three separate parties — the girls, their mother, and his wife — within a few streets of one another.

15 July 189516 St. Vincent St., Toronto

Alice and Nellie are found

Buried three feet deep in the cellar of a house Holmes rented for a fortnight, using a spade borrowed from the neighbour and returned.

20 July – August 1895Chicago

The building is opened, and the legend is born

Police excavate the basement while competing newspapers invent the Murder Castle in daily instalments: gas chambers, a crematorium, a body chute, a hundred victims. No Chicago charge ever follows. This is the version that survives.

27 August 1895Irvington, Ind.

Howard is found

Charred remains, teeth and a scorched tin toy recovered from the chimney and stove of a rented cottage. Carrie Pitezel identifies the toy.

19 August 1895Chicago

Fire guts the upper floors

The building burns during the excavation frenzy — widely suspected at the time to be an insurance play arranged in advance, and never satisfactorily explained.

28 October – 2 November 1895Philadelphia

Trial and conviction

Commonwealth v. Mudgett, before Judge Michael Arnold: one count, the murder of Benjamin Pitezel. Holmes dismisses his counsel and defends himself for part of it. The jury convicts of murder in the first degree in under three hours.

The end

1896
April 1896Moyamensing Prison

Sells a confession to 27 murders

Reportedly for around $7,500. Within weeks, named victims are found alive and the dates are shown to conflict with the record. Nearly every inflated body count in circulation descends from this document.

7 May 1896Philadelphia

Hanged

Nine days before his thirty-fifth birthday. He retracts the confession on the scaffold, claiming only two deaths. The drop does not kill him cleanly; he is pronounced dead about twenty minutes later. Buried in concrete, at his own request, at Holy Cross Cemetery, Yeadon.

The afterlife

1896 – present
1896Philadelphia

Geyer publishes his account

The Holmes-Pitezel Case: A History of the Greatest Crime of the Century — a plain, procedural narrative of the search, and still the most reliable document in the literature.

1938Chicago

The building is demolished

After four decades as a local curiosity with shops still trading below. A United States Post Office is later built on the site, where it remains.

1940s – 1990sPrint

The count inflates

Pulp magazines and mass-market true-crime paperbacks recycle the 1895 coverage, each edition rounding upward, until "up to 200 victims" is repeated as established fact by sources that cite only each other.

2003New York

The Devil in the White City

Erik Larson's bestseller interleaves Holmes with the architects of the 1893 exposition. Carefully sourced from the surviving 1890s press record, it is narrative history rather than forensic audit — and it permanently welds Holmes to the fair in popular memory.

2017Yeadon, Pa. / Chicago

The grave is opened; the record is re-examined

Court-authorised exhumation at the request of his descendants confirms by dental comparison that the man in the concrete is Holmes, ending the substitution rumour. The same year, Adam Selzer's document-based reconstruction dismantles much of the Castle legend from city records.

TodayEverywhere

The legend keeps its lead

The corrected account is freely available and thoroughly documented. The gas chamber and the two hundred victims remain, by an enormous margin, the more popular version — which is, in the end, the most Holmes-like fact about the whole affair.

Finally

Where all of this comes from

The sources behind every claim on this site, and how to check them yourself.

Sources & method
VII

Apparatus

Sources & method

A site that spends seven chapters telling you not to trust unsourced claims owes you its own workings. Here they are, including the parts that are weaker than one would like.

How claims are graded

Every substantive statement on this site sits in one of four bands. The bands are about evidence, not about how plausible something feels.

Evidence grading bands used across the archive
BandRequires
Documented Court records, official documents contemporaneous with the event, physical evidence, or multiple independent primary sources in agreement.
Probable Strong circumstantial evidence and/or several independent sources, but no conviction, body, or definitive document. Most of the Chicago disappearances sit here.
Disputed Credible researchers actively disagree, or the fact is established but its interpretation is not — as with the building's blind rooms and shaft.
Invention Traceable to a specific piece of sensational reporting, pulp writing, or self-serving confession, with no independent support.

Three rules applied throughout

  • Holmes is not a source about Holmes. His memoir and confessions are quoted as artefacts of his behaviour, never as evidence of events.
  • 1895 newspapers are evidence of 1895 newspapers. They are indispensable for reconstructing what was said and when the legend formed, and unreliable for what was in the basement.
  • Absence of a body is not absence of a crime — but it does cap a claim at "probable", which is why five of the nine names in the register carry that mark rather than a higher one.

Limitations of this archive

This is a secondary synthesis written for general readers, not original archival research. It has not consulted the Philadelphia court files, Chicago building permits, or Fidelity Mutual's records directly; it relies on published scholarship that has. Dates for undocumented disappearances are approximate by necessity. The floor plans are interpretive reconstructions — no complete original drawing of the building is known to survive, and every published plan, including the famous 1895 newspaper diagrams, is somebody's interpretation.

Where this site says "probably" or "appears to", that is the honest state of the evidence and not hedging for style.

Bibliography

Sources, with their weaknesses stated

Roughly in order of evidentiary weight, not alphabetically.

  1. Adam Selzer, H. H. Holmes: The True History of the White City Devil (Skyhorse, 2017) Documentary research

    The single most important corrective work on the case. Built from Chicago building and licensing records, city directories, court filings, and a systematic reading of the 1890s press against itself. It is the basis for most of the myth-check verdicts on this site, including the finding that the "World's Fair Hotel" cannot be shown to have operated.
    Weakness: a revisionist project by design, and occasionally more confident in its negatives than the surviving record strictly allows.

  2. Frank P. Geyer, The Holmes-Pitezel Case: A History of the Greatest Crime of the Century (Philadelphia, 1896) Primary · public domain

    The investigating detective's own account of the search for the Pitezel children, written immediately afterwards. Plain, procedural, dated, and specific about places and witnesses. Everything this site says about Cincinnati, Indianapolis, Detroit, Toronto and Irvington rests on it.
    Weakness: written by a participant, for a public audience, shortly after the events, and not neutral about its subject.

  3. Trial record, Commonwealth of Pennsylvania v. Herman W. Mudgett, alias H. H. Holmes, Court of Oyer and Terminer, Philadelphia County, October–November 1895 Primary · court record

    The only judicial determination ever made about any of Holmes's killings. Published transcripts and contemporaneous digests supply the medical evidence on the chloroform, the identification testimony, and the conduct of the defence.
    Weakness: its scope is one murder. It is silent on Chicago, which is precisely why so much about Chicago is unresolved.

  4. H. H. Holmes, Holmes' Own Story (1895) and the confession published in the Hearst press, April 1896 Primary · unreliable

    Both written for money, both self-serving, mutually contradictory, and repudiated by their own author on the scaffold. Several people named as victims were subsequently found alive.
    Use: evidence of how Holmes presented himself and of how the inflated body counts entered circulation. Not evidence of events.

  5. Contemporaneous newspaper coverage: Chicago Tribune, Chicago Times-Herald, Chicago Inter Ocean, Philadelphia Inquirer, New York World, July 1895 – May 1896 Primary · sensational

    Indispensable for dating the formation of the legend almost hour by hour, and for showing features appearing in one edition that were absent from the previous day's account of the same room.
    Weakness: circulation-driven competition with minimal verification. This is the origin point of most of the enduring myths.

  6. Erik Larson, The Devil in the White City (Crown, 2003) Narrative history

    The book responsible for the modern shape of the story, interleaving Holmes with Daniel Burnham and the 1893 exposition. Carefully sourced and openly referenced, and a genuinely superb piece of writing.
    Weakness: it draws heavily on the surviving 1890s press record, which carries that record's distortions forward; and its structural pairing of the fair with the killer is a literary device that readers have widely absorbed as a documented connection.

  7. Harold Schechter, Depraved: The Definitive True Story of H. H. Holmes (1994; rev. 2004) Secondary

    The standard full-length treatment before the 2017 revisions, thorough on the Pitezel case and the trial.
    Weakness: largely pre-dates the systematic records work, and accepts several Castle claims that have since been substantially undercut.

  8. Court-authorised exhumation and forensic identification, Holy Cross Cemetery, Yeadon, Pennsylvania, 2017 (University of Pennsylvania forensic anthropology team) Physical evidence

    Undertaken at the request of Holmes's descendants. The coffin was cut out of solid cement; dental comparison identified the remains as Holmes, closing the "he escaped the gallows" theory.

  9. Civil records: U.S. Federal Census 1870–1900; Michigan and New Hampshire vital records; Cook County property and licensing records; Chicago city directories Primary · public

    The ordinary paperwork that decides most of the disputed points — including Elizabeth Holton's survival, the marriage dates, the medical degree, and the absence of a hotel licence in operation.

✦

Corrections

If something here is wrong, it should be fixed rather than defended. This is a static site kept in a public repository; corrections belong in the repository's issue tracker, with a source attached. Claims that arrive without a source will be held to the same standard as the ones this site spends seven chapters rejecting.

On tone

This archive deliberately avoids the aesthetic that usually attends this material — the leering reconstructions, the invented interior monologue, the murderer as antihero. Four of the nine people listed here were children. The design is dark because the subject is; it is not dark because the subject is entertaining.
